language_wrapper: Consider the integers n between 1 and {alpha}, inclusive. How many of these n can be written in at least {rho} distinct ways as a difference of the squares of two nonnegative integers a and b with a > b ≥ 0? (Each ordered pair (a, b) with a ≥ b and a^2 − b^2 = n counts as one representation.)
hardness_rationale: The seed problem relies on the simple characterization a^2 − b^2 = (a − b)(a + b) and reduces to excluding integers congruent to 2 mod 4. Our augmentation requires counting, for each n, how many distinct representations exist with b > 0, which corresponds to counting unordered factor pairs subject to a parity constraint. This transforms the task into analyzing the divisor function of n (or n/4) and aggregating conditions across an interval, introducing multiplicity, perfect-square edge cases, and parity-driven reductions. The solution thus demands a structured factorization-to-divisor-count argument and a more sophisticated global counting over [1, alpha], rather than a single modular exclusion.
notes: Proof outline for the family: For any nonnegative integers a ≥ b, write n = a^2 − b^2 = (a − b)(a + b) = uv with u = a − b > 0, v = a + b > 0. Conversely, given u, v of the same parity with uv = n and u ≤ v, we obtain integers a = (u + v)/2, b = (v − u)/2 ≥ 0. Thus representations with a > b ≥ 0 are in bijection with unordered factor pairs (u, v) of n having u and v of the same parity, with the additional restriction b > 0 excluding the central pair u = v. When n is odd, all factors are odd, so the number of such representations equals floor(tau(n)/2). When n ≡ 0 (mod 4), write n = 4m; admissible pairs (u, v) are both even, so after factoring out 2, we count unordered factor pairs of m, again yielding floor(tau(m)/2). When n ≡ 2 (mod 4), no such pairs exist. Therefore, letting f(n) denote the number of representations with b > 0, we have: f(n) = 0 if n ≡ 2 (mod 4); f(n) = floor(tau(n)/2) if n is odd; and f(n) = floor(tau(n/4)/2) if n ≡ 0 (mod 4). The problem reduces to counting n ≤ alpha with f(n) ≥ rho. The generator/verifier implement this logic and guard against trivial instances by ensuring rho ≥ 2 and the resulting count is neither 0 nor alpha.
source_question: How many of the integers between 1 and 1000, inclusive, can be expressed as the difference of the squares of two nonnegative integers?
